Tap the beam’s top edge, right under the load, so the crosshair’s horizontal line lies along the edge. Pinch or double-tap to zoom in first; drag to move around.
Now tap the bottom edge. The mark stays on the vertical line, so only its height follows your tap.

Only %1$d px across: a 1 px slip changes E by about %2$d%%. Zoom in, or photograph the middle of the beam closer.

Import the loads as a CSV, in N or kN: the file the testing machine exported, or one you type yourself with one load per photo, in the same order as the photos. A longer machine log is matched by time for video frames, or spread evenly over the photos. Loads keep their sign.

Stress = load ÷ cross-section area. For a round bar the area is π × d² ÷ 4 (d = diameter in mm). Strain comes from the photos, so no extensometer is needed. The strain axis is the direction the bar is pulled in the image.

Young’s modulus E is the slope of the straight, early part of the curve, so take several photos before the bar starts to yield. E from a phone camera is approximate; compare it with the value your lab gives you.

Import the loads as a CSV in N or kN, one per photo in the same order as the photos. A hanger load in kg is kg × 9.81 N.

Point the phone at the side of the beam, at the middle where the load hangs, on a tripod. Take the reference photo with no load on the hanger — that is the dial gauge’s zero. Frame the middle of the beam rather than the whole span, so the thickness covers plenty of pixels.

After the dimensions, tap the beam’s top and bottom edges under the load on the reference photo: the thickness you measured over those pixels is the photo’s scale, and the deflection δ is read there.

Bending stress σb = M·y ÷ I, with M = W·L ÷ 4, y = t ÷ 2 and I = b·t³ ÷ 12 (L span, b width, t thickness). E = W·L³ ÷ (48·δ·I) for each load, and also from the slope of the load–deflection graph. E from a phone camera is approximate.
